items.good: The reader finds the opening right under the name with no heading, beginning with the idea (one folder per kind, by extension, listing before moving, never deleting, renaming or overwriting, and undo), then whom it is for; then Example, Why organize-downloads, Requirements, Installation, Documentation, Development and License in the template's order and headings. Each section opens with its main point, each Requirements item is one sentence alone with its explanation indented after a blank line, and no item is bold.

From the opening the reader learns the idea that sets the tool apart (sorting by each file's extension, a listing first, and moves that never delete, rename or overwrite and can be undone), that it is a command-line tool for macOS and Linux, and that it is for anyone whose Downloads folder holds so many files they cannot find the one they want, so they can place themselves.

The reader sees a Downloads folder like their own, the listing it prints, the --move run and the folder after it, the --undo run with its lines and the folder back as at first, with each case shown (a name already taken, an unknown kind, hidden files, downloads in progress, a folder already there), how to work on another folder, and the table of every kind's extensions.

The reader sees, set against sorting by hand, sorting the view in a file manager, and a rule-based organizer, the work each leaves them that this tool does: making the folders and moving the files, putting files in folders rather than ordering a view, and coming with its kinds already set.

Not met at the design stage; to be checked at the build stage. What the README gives now: each requirement said as what it is before one way of getting it: Python 3.8 or later run as python3, with how to get it on macOS and, through the package manager such as `sudo apt install python3` on Debian or Ubuntu, on a Linux system without it; curl; and ~/.local/bin in PATH, with the startup file told by the shell. Each of these steps works as written here: python3 --version printed Python 3.14.4, apt offers the python3 package, curl is at /usr/bin/curl, and echo "$SHELL" names the shell. It also gives the download into ~/.local/bin, making it runnable, --help, the first use as the Example's three runs, and the macOS note on Downloads access. What waits: the download address gives 404, as the tool's file organize-downloads/organize-downloads does not exist yet. So installing and running --help and the Example are checked by a first user installing from that address once the build stage has made the tool and put it on main, as the CCS chooses and the user decided.

Not met at the design stage; to be checked at the build stage. What the README gives now: fuller use named at docs/usage.md and the changes of each version at CHANGELOG.md under Documentation, the builders' entrance docs/architecture.md alone under Development, and the license named as MIT with a link to LICENSE, which is there with the MIT text and "Copyright (c) 2026 lovaizu". What waits: docs/usage.md and CHANGELOG.md are made with the tool in the build stage, and docs/architecture.md by T2; the links name where they will be, and are checked once those files are on main.

parts.good: The reader takes in what the tool does, how, and for whom in two sentences of common words, each resting on nothing later.

The reader follows the folder, each run and its output in blocks, in order, each case named with what happens in it right where it shows (why two files have no line, why budget.xlsx stays, what --undo removes and keeps, what a file that cannot go back does), and the extensions in a table after the rule that matches them.
The reader reads the main point first, then each other way as one item with the work it leaves them, resting only on the Example's table above.

The reader reads each requirement as what it is, with why and how to check it, how to get Python on macOS and on Linux, each command in a block to copy, and the startup file told from the shell by a command given there.
The reader reads the install commands in one block, then --help, then the first use as the Example's three runs, with the macOS access prompt and what to do about it.
The reader reads two items, each saying what is written where, with its link.
The builder reads in one sentence where how the tool is made and tested is written.
The reader reads the license's name and where its terms are.
The reader reads the standard MIT text, known on sight, with its copyright line.

items.good: Each sentence gives the reader something no other gives: the opening's gain is not said again in Why, which sets the tool against other ways; Installation's first use points to the Example's runs rather than repeating them; the --move run says it prints the same five lines rather than showing them again; nothing speaks to a reviewer, tells history, or holds fuller use.

Not met at the design stage; to be checked at the build stage. What the README gives now: its statements agree with one another and with AC1-AC12. Never deleting, renaming or overwriting holds in the Example, as budget.xlsx stays and --undo removes only empty folders the move made. Undo of the last run that moved files agrees with the --undo lines. Folders already there are left as they are in the trees. Each kind's folder has one name throughout, and there is no "not yet" or "for now". The Requirements commands hold when run here. What waits: what --help prints, the Python 3.8 floor, macOS, the three runs' output and trees, the undo lines for a file that cannot go back, and case handling of extensions are checked against the tool by a first user once the build stage has made it and put it on main.

chosen.chosen: LICENSE holds the standard MIT text as the Open Source Initiative gives it, headed "MIT License", with only the decided copyright line filled in.
chosen.why: The decision names the MIT license and its copyright line; the standard text unchanged is what readers and tools recognise as MIT.

chosen.chosen: The download address is https://raw.githubusercontent.com/lovaizu/playground/main/organize-downloads/organize-downloads, the tool's single file named organize-downloads in the organize-downloads folder of main, fetched with curl.
chosen.why: The decision says the file is downloaded into ~/.local/bin; steering.md's pull request is in lovaizu/playground, a raw address on main serves the file as it is, and naming the file as the command means it runs by that name without renaming; curl is on macOS and most Linux systems.

chosen.chosen: Python 3.8 or later is the version the README asks for.
chosen.why: The decision says Python 3 with only its standard library and names no version; 3.8 sets a floor low enough for older systems still in use, which I have not checked against a list of systems, and the tool is to use nothing a later standard library alone gives.

chosen.chosen: For a Linux system without Python, the README says to install it with the system's package manager, giving `sudo apt install python3` on Debian or Ubuntu as the example, in the same form as the curl item.
chosen.why: The first user found nothing for a Linux system without Python; python3 is the package's name on Debian and Ubuntu (apt offers it here), and the same form as curl's item lets the reader read both alike.

chosen.chosen: The options are --move and --undo, with the folder given after the options and ~/Downloads when none is given, and each line's wording is as the Example shows ("name -> Folder/", "name: stays, <why>", "name: back from Folder/").
chosen.why: steering.md names an option that moves and one that undoes but not their names or the lines' wording; short words that say the action let the reader type them from memory, and the README is what the build and T2 make the tool to.

chosen.chosen: The full list of extensions of each kind is the table in the Example: the steering.md examples plus jpeg, heif, bmp, tif, tiff; doc, xls, ppt, odt, ods, odp, rtf, pages, numbers, key; tgz, bz2, xz; aac, flac, ogg, opus, aiff; avi, webm, m4v, matched in capitals or small letters alike by the part after the last dot.
chosen.why: AC2 leaves the full list to the design and T1 to hold it; these are the common files of each kind met in a Downloads folder on macOS and Linux, and matching the last dot gives archive.tar.gz to Archives with one rule.

chosen.chosen: The PATH line is added to the shell's startup file, ~/.zshrc for zsh and ~/.bashrc for bash, each named with the system that starts it by default, and `echo "$SHELL"` tells the reader which shell they have.
chosen.why: zsh and bash are the shells macOS and most Linux systems start by default, so a newcomer with no setup of their own finds the right file, and a reader on the other shell, such as zsh on Linux, can tell the file from their shell rather than their system.

chosen.chosen: The first use tells macOS readers that macOS may ask whether the terminal may access the Downloads folder, and to allow it.
chosen.why: macOS guards the Downloads folder and asks the first time a terminal reads it; a reader who refuses gets no files listed and cannot tell why, and the README says "may" since a terminal already allowed is not asked.

chosen.chosen: The opening says the tool "can undo its last run that moved files in that folder", keeping "move" for one file's move.
chosen.why: The opening already uses "move" for one file's move ("every move it would make"), and steering.md's G1 speaks of undoing "the last run that moved files"; one word for each thing lets the reader tell them apart.

chosen.chosen: For the --move run, the Example keeps the words that it prints the same five lines as the run above and shows only the command in its block, rather than showing the five lines again.
chosen.why: The first user found the two saying one thing; keeping the words tells the reader at once that nothing differs, where a second block would have them compare it line by line, and the command still stands in a block to copy.
